# ADR-1107: The SessionStart curation sample sorts three narrow columns, not whole rows

## Status

accepted

## Context

`_count_pending_curations` (ADR-0498) samples the 500 most recently accessed live memories with `SELECT m.id, m.content, m.tags, effective_heat(m, NOW()), m.created_at, m.domain FROM memories m JOIN current_memories cm ON cm.id = m.id WHERE NOT m.is_stale ORDER BY m.last_accessed DESC NULLS LAST, m.created_at DESC LIMIT 500`. On the owner's store (68,496 memories; heap 944 MB) EXPLAIN ANALYZE on 2026-10-14 showed `Parallel Seq Scan on memories` (plan width 1774) feeding a `Sort` that carries content, tags and the other columns as payload: `Sort Method: external merge`, 127 MB, 128 MB and 130 MB spilled to disk by the leader and the two workers (a Sort under a Gather Merge is not bounded by the LIMIT). Execution Time 55,343 ms the first time (cold) and 13,423 ms the second; measured again later that day with the pages cached, 2,371 ms and 1,205 ms, spills of 125 to 134 MB each. It is the largest single cost of the warm SessionStart hook (3.5 s of its 6.3 s; its 9 psycopg executes total 4.9 s).

## Decision

Choose the 500 on the three narrow columns that order them, then read only those rows whole: `SELECT ... FROM (SELECT id FROM memories WHERE NOT is_stale AND superseded_by_id IS NULL ORDER BY last_accessed DESC NULLS LAST, created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 500) newest JOIN memories m ON m.id = newest.id ORDER BY m.last_accessed DESC NULLS LAST, m.created_at DESC, m.id DESC`. `NOT is_stale AND superseded_by_id IS NULL` is what `JOIN current_memories ... WHERE NOT m.is_stale` kept (the view's own filter is `superseded_by_id IS NULL`, seen in the old plan); `id DESC` makes the cut deterministic when two rows share both timestamps. **No index on `last_accessed`.** One was built and measured (`(last_accessed DESC NULLS LAST, created_at DESC, id DESC) WHERE NOT is_stale AND superseded_by_id IS NULL`: 9.9 to 22.7 ms against 91 to 182 ms without it, on a packed copy of the table) and rejected: `update_memory_access` writes `last_accessed` and `access_count` for every memory a recall returns, and PostgreSQL ends heap-only (HOT) updates for a row once an indexed column changes (documentation, "Heap-Only Tuples"), so every recall would add an entry to each of the table's 25 indexes, the HNSW and the two GIN text indexes included, to save ~130 ms once per session; that write cost was not measured, and the rewrite alone meets the goal.

## Consequences

Measured with EXPLAIN ANALYZE, read-only on the owner's live store: the new statement takes 146 ms and 157 ms (a `Parallel Seq Scan` over three columns, top-N heapsort of 82 to 88 kB, no spill) against 1,205 to 2,371 ms for the old statement run in the same session (13,423 and 55,343 ms in its first two runs). The 500 ids of the old statement (with the same tie-break) and of the new one, run read-only on the live store, are byte-identical in order. The scan still reads the whole heap (944 MB on this store; a packed pg_dump copy of the same rows is 104 MB, so the live heap is about 9 times bloated), so the cost grows with the table: a user with many more memories pays it each session, and the index is the answer if that becomes the measured problem, weighed against the recall write path then. The other eight statements of the SessionStart hook (1.4 s together) are not changed here. A PostgreSQL regression test seeds wide rows under the plan settings of the measured plan and fails when the sample spills to disk.
